paragraphs: This paper examines whether copyright detection systems can be evaded through deliberately chosen changes to audio. These systems help identify copyrighted material online, so their vulnerability has consequences beyond ordinary classification errors. The authors investigate whether adversarial perturbations can undermine the identification process, including in industrial tools.

Their proof of concept starts with a known music identification method, implemented as a neural network. This representation lets them use gradient information to construct changes that interfere with recognition. They show that the resulting system is easily defeated in the white-box setting, where the attacker has access to the model being attacked.

The authors then increase the perturbations to produce attacks that transfer to AudioTag and YouTube’s Content ID. These changes are audible, so the result does not establish imperceptible evasion of those services. However, the perturbations are substantially smaller than a random baseline. The findings demonstrate a practical vulnerability in the tested systems and motivate strengthening copyright detection against deliberately constructed inputs.
icml-2020-adversarial-attacks-on-copyrig.tldr: Deliberately constructed audio perturbations defeat a music identification model and transfer to industrial copyright detectors, although the transferred changes are audible.

paragraphs: Larger models can improve average test performance while making predictions worse for minority groups. This paper studies that pattern when training data contains spurious correlations: associations that a model can exploit but that do not serve all groups equally. It focuses on increasing model size beyond what is already sufficient to achieve zero training error.

Through simulations and experiments on two image datasets, the authors identify two important influences: the relative sizes of majority and minority groups, and the signal-to-noise ratio of the spurious correlations. They also analyze a linear setting. There, they show theoretically how a preference for solutions that memorize fewer examples can make additional model capacity harmful.

The analysis motivates reducing the number of majority-group training examples. Empirically, this approach achieves low minority-group error in the overparameterized regime, even where increasing minority examples’ training weights fails. The result suggests that retaining all available training data can conflict with achieving low worst-group error in these settings. It does not imply that larger models or additional data always harm minority groups.
icml-2020-an-investigation-of-why-overpa.tldr: The paper explains how spurious correlations can make larger models worse for minority groups and shows that subsampling the majority can help.

paragraphs: Group convolutional networks learn representations built around symmetry patterns. The authors identify a missing capability: these networks do not explicitly learn which relationships among those patterns are meaningful. Recognizing symmetry alone does not directly express whether particular relative positions or poses form a useful combination.

The paper introduces attentive group equivariant convolutions, which incorporate attention into the convolution operation itself. Attention emphasizes useful combinations of symmetry patterns and reduces the influence of combinations that are implausible or misleading. This generalizes group convolution while retaining the framework’s focus on symmetry. The authors also describe earlier visual attention approaches as special cases of the proposed formulation.

On benchmark image datasets, the resulting networks consistently outperform conventional group convolutional networks in the reported experiments. The method also produces equivariant attention maps that can be visualized to help interpret learned concepts. Together, these results support learning relationships among symmetry patterns as a useful addition to learning the patterns themselves, with attention providing both a modeling mechanism and a way to inspect what the network emphasizes.
icml-2020-attentive-group-equivariant-co.tldr: Adding attention within group convolutions improves reported image benchmark performance and makes relationships among learned symmetry patterns easier to inspect.

paragraphs: Many black-box optimization problems involve both numerical settings and categorical choices. Existing approaches can struggle when several categorical variables each have many possible values. One-hot encoding expands the search space, while building separate models for different categories uses observations inefficiently because information is divided across those models.

The proposed method, CoCaBO, combines multi-armed bandits with Bayesian optimization to choose categorical and continuous inputs. A Gaussian process kernel models the mixed input space and allows information to be shared across multiple categorical variables. This sharing is central to the approach: available observations can inform the search without requiring a separate, isolated model for every categorical configuration.

The authors also extend CoCaBO to select batches of evaluations. Their selection procedure adjusts the balance between exploring uncertain choices and exploiting promising ones while encouraging diversity within a batch. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show better performance than existing approaches in the tested settings. The findings support treating mixed inputs jointly and sharing information across categories as a practical route to more efficient optimization.
icml-2020-bayesian-optimisation-over-mul.tldr: CoCaBO combines bandits and Bayesian optimization to search mixed categorical and continuous spaces while sharing information across categorical choices.

paragraphs: Similarity search uses compact representations to help find related items. FlyHash, inspired by the fruit fly’s smell-processing circuitry, takes an unusual approach: it produces high-dimensional codes with relatively few active entries. Although FlyHash has shown strong empirical performance, its random projections cannot adapt to the data being searched.

This paper introduces BioHash, which learns sparse, high-dimensional hash codes from data. Its learning rule updates connections locally and is described as biologically plausible. The method therefore combines the expansive representation that motivated FlyHash with a mechanism for adapting that representation. The authors also introduce BioConvHash, a convolutional variant that further improves performance.

BioHash outperforms previously published hashing benchmarks in the reported evaluation. Both proposed methods are described as fast and scalable, producing compressed binary representations useful for similarity search. The biological interpretation is more tentative: the results provide evidence that locality-sensitive hashing could help explain why sparse, expansive representations occur in biological systems. They support that computational explanation without establishing it as the sole purpose of those biological structures.
icml-2020-bio-inspired-hashing-for-unsup.tldr: BioHash learns sparse, high-dimensional binary codes for similarity search, improving reported hashing benchmarks and supporting a possible computational role for biological sparse representations.

paragraphs: Evaluating a classifier usually requires more access than is available in this paper’s setting. There may be no validation set, or the classifier itself may be inaccessible even for queries. Instead, the available evidence consists of each subpopulation’s positive prediction rate and its true positive-label rate.

The authors show how these aggregate statistics can establish a lower bound on discrepancy, a measure combining inaccuracy and unfairness. They introduce an unfairness measure based on the fraction of the population where the classifier’s behavior differs from its globally fair behavior under equalized odds. This turns population-level information into a constraint on how favorable the classifier’s combined accuracy and fairness could be.

An efficient procedure computes the strongest discrepancy lower bound supported by the supplied aggregate statistics. Experiments demonstrate empirical tightness and illustrate applications involving voting polls and patient identification from internet searches. A lower bound identifies a minimum amount of discrepancy consistent with the evidence; it does not recover every individual prediction or fully determine the classifier’s behavior. That makes the method useful when direct evaluation is unavailable.
icml-2020-bounding-the-fairness-and-accu.tldr: Aggregate prediction and label rates can yield tight lower bounds on a classifier’s combined inaccuracy and unfairness without direct classifier access.

paragraphs: A dataset can combine observations generated by several different causal models. This paper studies mixtures in which each component model is represented by a directed acyclic graph. The component responsible for an observation is hidden, making structure discovery a problem involving an unobserved mixing variable.

The authors construct a graphical representation for the mixture distribution and prove that it encodes the distribution’s conditional independence relationships. They then examine structure-learning algorithms that accommodate latent variables, including FCI. Their analysis shows that these algorithms recover a union of the component graphs and can identify variables whose conditional distributions differ across components.

Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the inferred graph identifies nodes that vary between mixture components. The authors also show how this causal information can help cluster observations by their generating component. The contribution connects a description of dependencies in mixed data with information about where the underlying mechanisms change. The recovered union provides a combined structural view rather than simply presenting a separate complete graph for every hidden component.
icml-2020-causal-structure-discovery-fro.tldr: The paper characterizes causal mixtures graphically and shows how latent-variable discovery methods can recover combined structure and identify changing mechanisms.

paragraphs: Training-data poisoning changes the data used to build a classifier rather than only altering an input at prediction time. This paper develops a general view of randomized smoothing over arbitrary functions and uses it to construct classifiers with pointwise certificates against poisoning. Each certificate concerns the stability of a particular test prediction.

The concrete application builds linear classifiers resistant to label flipping. For each test example, the certificate guarantees that its prediction would remain unchanged if some number of training labels had been adversarially modified. The attack model permits a different targeted attack for each test point. This is a prediction-invariance guarantee, rather than a statement that the unchanged prediction must be correct.

The authors derive a deterministic analytical bound, avoiding the probabilistic certificates associated with sampling-based smoothing procedures. They report minimal additional runtime complexity relative to standard classification and require no assumptions about training or test distributions. They also extend the results to multiple classes, presenting what they identify as the first multiclass classification algorithm with certified robustness to label-flipping attacks.
icml-2020-certified-robustness-to-label-.tldr: A smoothing framework provides deterministic, per-prediction certificates that linear classifiers withstand a bounded number of adversarial training-label changes.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose among models that predict conditional average treatment effects, or CATE. These models estimate how an average treatment effect varies with the characteristics being considered. The authors focus on model selection: an evaluation procedure needs to distinguish stronger candidate predictors from weaker ones reliably.

Their central objective is to preserve the ordering of candidates by performance. This places attention on whether an evaluation metric ranks models correctly, which directly determines which model gets selected. The authors analyze the ranking problem and derive guidelines for constructing a better metric. They then propose a metric designed to identify the performance ordering of CATE predictors with high confidence.

Empirical evaluations show that the proposed metric outperforms existing metrics for both selecting models and tuning hyperparameters. These are two settings where a reliable ordering helps choose among competing predictors or configurations. The stated contribution is therefore an improved evaluation and selection procedure for causal inference models, with theoretical analysis informing the metric and experiments supporting its usefulness for the tested selection tasks.
icml-2020-counterfactual-cross-validatio.tldr: A new evaluation metric improves CATE model selection by focusing on reliably ranking candidate predictors by performance.

paragraphs: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm is a first-order method for drawing samples from log-concave probability distributions. This paper changes its step-size schedule through annealing. The contribution centers on how that schedule enables convergence guarantees for smooth log-concave distributions that are not covered by the existing guarantees discussed by the authors.

To prove these results, the authors establish a new relationship between Wasserstein distance and total variation distance for any two log-concave distributions. These are different ways to measure how far probability distributions are from one another. Connecting them supplies a theoretical tool for the sampling analysis and complements the range of situations addressed by Talagrand’s T2 inequality.

The authors also apply the schedule to an existing algorithm for sampling under constraints. In that setting, they obtain state-of-the-art convergence rates and improve how the guarantees depend on dimension. The significance is both algorithmic and analytical: a step-size choice expands the available convergence results, while the new distance bound helps justify them. The stated guarantees concern the specified log-concave sampling settings.
icml-2020-double-loop-unadjusted-langevi.tldr: A new annealing schedule for Langevin sampling yields additional convergence guarantees and improves dimension dependence for constrained log-concave sampling.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine model updates from distributed clients, making communication a bottleneck. Sparse client participation creates an additional challenge for convergence. FetchSGD addresses these problems together by compressing updates and changing where information used across training steps is maintained.

The algorithm compresses each model update using a Count Sketch. These sketches can be merged, allowing the central aggregator to combine compressed updates from many workers. Crucially, Count Sketch is linear, so momentum and accumulated compression errors can be maintained within the sketch itself. FetchSGD therefore moves those operations from individual clients to the aggregator, reducing the difficulty posed by clients that participate only occasionally.

The authors prove favorable convergence guarantees and evaluate the method by training two residual networks and a transformer. They report effective training alongside high compression rates. The main design insight is that compression need not be treated only as a way to shrink messages: its mathematical structure also determines which training operations can be centralized. Here, that structure supports both communication efficiency and handling sparse participation.
icml-2020-fetchsgd-communication-efficie.tldr: FetchSGD uses mergeable sketches to compress federated updates and maintain momentum and accumulated errors centrally despite sparse client participation.

paragraphs: Continuous-time optimization describes a changing state through differential equations or differential inclusions. This paper asks when such a system reaches a minimum in finite time. The distinction matters mathematically: approaching a minimum indefinitely is different from reaching it after a finite amount of continuous evolution.

The authors study a Lyapunov-like differential inequality that establishes finite-time stability. Using this condition, they construct first- and second-order dynamical systems that converge in finite time to minima of sufficiently regular cost functions. The inequality acts as a tool for designing optimization dynamics as well as analyzing their behavior.

They also prove finite-time convergence for p-rescaled gradient flow when the cost function is gradient dominated of order q, with q strictly between 1 and p. This conditional result connects that flow with normalized gradient flow, corresponding to the infinite-p case. Finally, the paper discusses discretization strategies and supplies numerical illustrations. Its principal guarantees concern continuous-time systems under the stated regularity and gradient-domination conditions; the discussion of discretization addresses how those flows might inform computational methods.
icml-2020-finite-time-convergence-in-con.tldr: A differential inequality enables continuous-time optimization systems with finite-time convergence under stated regularity conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify a good or winning item from noisy comparisons governed by the Plackett-Luce model. Each comparison tests a fixed-size subset and returns top-ranked feedback. The objective is to make the required number of observations depend on the difficulty of the particular collection of items.

The authors wrap a winner-finding algorithm with weaker guarantees in a procedure that adapts to instance difficulty. Their sample-complexity bound depends on the gaps between the best item and its competitors, the subset size, and the strength of the top items. They also show a multiplicative improvement when each comparison supplies a longer ranked list. Matching lower bounds establish the stated optimality of their algorithms.

The paper additionally considers a fixed-budget setting, where the learner must choose a winner after a prescribed number of comparisons. Here, the authors derive instance-dependent upper and lower bounds on the probability of selecting the wrong item. Numerical results accompany the theory. Together, the analyses characterize both the observations needed for reliable identification and the error possible when observations are limited.
icml-2020-from-pac-to-instance-optimal-s.tldr: Adaptive winner-finding algorithms achieve instance-optimal sample complexity for Plackett-Luce comparisons, with further gains from longer ranked feedback.

paragraphs: Integer submodular functions describe objectives over discrete quantities, extending the setting beyond simple set membership. Such objectives arise in problems including budget allocation, multilabel graph cuts, and revenue maximization with discrete assignments. This paper develops their use in probabilistic modeling, an area the authors identify as receiving less attention than optimization.

The first contribution is a Generalized Multilinear Extension: a continuous extension of integer submodular functions that has a diminishing-returns property. The authors study its central mathematical properties and introduce a probabilistic model defined through integer submodular functions. The continuous formulation provides a connection between the discrete structure of the model and the machinery used to work with it.

For approximate inference, the paper introduces a block-coordinate ascent algorithm, which updates blocks of variables in turn. Evaluations on real-world social connection graphs with integer submodular objectives demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness and viability. The contribution combines a model class, an extension with useful mathematical structure, and an inference procedure, bringing integer-valued submodular objectives into a probabilistic framework.
icml-2020-from-sets-to-multisets-provabl.tldr: The paper introduces probabilistic integer submodular models, a continuous extension, and a block-coordinate method for approximate inference.

paragraphs: Sleeping bandits model sequential choices where some actions are temporarily unavailable, such as recommending products that may be out of stock. This paper considers randomly generated availability sets alongside adversarial rewards. The learner must make effective choices while respecting whichever actions are available at each round.

Previously, efficient algorithms guaranteed regret growing as T to the two-thirds power, while computationally inefficient approaches could achieve square-root growth in T. The authors introduce an efficient algorithm inspired by EXP3 that achieves O(sqrt(T)) regret when individual actions’ availabilities are independent. Under that assumption, the result obtains the better time dependence without requiring an inefficient algorithm.

The paper also treats availability sets drawn from an unknown arbitrary distribution, removing independence between actions. For this broader setting, it provides an efficient algorithm with O(sqrt(2^K T)) regret, where K is the number of actions. The guarantee retains square-root dependence on the number of rounds but has an exponential dependence on action count inside the square root. Experimental evaluations corroborate the theoretical results.
icml-2020-improved-sleeping-bandits-with.tldr: An efficient sleeping-bandit algorithm achieves square-root regret under independent availability, with a broader guarantee for arbitrarily distributed action sets.

paragraphs: Deep Q-networks struggle with high-dimensional continuous actions because representing combinations of discretized actions can require a combinatorial number of outputs. One response is to divide the network into action modules. This paper examines how the arrangement of those modules affects the model’s ability to control a system.

The authors describe weaknesses in two established arrangements. Parallel modules lack coordination, which adds complexity to the task. Sequential modules can encounter vanishing gradients and a rapidly expanding parameter space. Their proposed method infers the network’s compositional structure using uncertainty-estimation techniques introduced in the paper, making module organization part of the solution rather than treating it as a fixed design choice.

The authors show that compositional structure substantially affects performance. Their method achieves state-of-the-art results on the tested MuJoCo environments with high-dimensional continuous actions, and they also demonstrate improvement in a realistic AAA sailing simulator game. These findings support adapting the relationships among action modules as a useful way to improve DQN control in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-inferring-dqn-structure-for-hi.tldr: Inferring how DQN action modules connect using uncertainty estimates improves reported performance on high-dimensional continuous-control tasks.

paragraphs: Inter-domain Gaussian processes offer flexible, relatively inexpensive approximate inference and are useful for modeling global structure. The authors identify a limitation in the shallow formulation they consider: stationary covariance functions make it difficult to capture non-stationary data, where statistical patterns change across the input space.

The proposed Inter-domain Deep Gaussian Processes combine inter-domain modeling with deep Gaussian processes. This brings the benefits of inter-domain features into a deeper model intended to handle the challenging data structure. The authors also show how existing approximate-inference methods can be used with these features, providing a simple and scalable inference approach for the combined model.

The method is evaluated on regression tasks, including challenging large-scale real-world datasets containing both global structure and substantial non-stationarity. In these evaluations, it outperforms both shallow inter-domain Gaussian processes and conventional deep Gaussian processes. The results support combining the two approaches when both kinds of structure matter, rather than relying on either component alone. The reported advantage is empirical on the evaluated datasets.
icml-2020-inter-domain-deep-gaussian-pro.tldr: Inter-domain deep Gaussian processes combine scalable inference with improved modeling of datasets containing global structure and non-stationarity.

paragraphs: Machine learning researchers have developed many definitions of fairness in response to harmful bias in applications such as hiring, medicine, and criminal justice. Some definitions draw on legal or ethical ideas, while others are primarily mathematical. This paper asks whether people outside the field understand basic fairness definitions.

The authors develop a metric for measuring comprehension of three definitions: demographic parity, equal opportunity, and equalized odds. They evaluate that metric through an online survey. They also investigate how comprehension relates to respondents’ sentiment, their demographics, and the particular fairness definition being presented.

The contribution is a way to study understanding as a distinct part of the relationship between technical fairness research and the public. Agreement with a definition and comprehension of it are different questions, and the study examines factors associated with comprehension. The abstract presents this as an initial step toward connecting researchers and non-experts; it does not report which definition was best understood or which demographic groups performed differently. Its stated contribution centers on measurement and the survey investigation.
icml-2020-measuring-non-expert-comprehen.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates a survey-based measure of non-experts’ understanding of three machine learning fairness definitions.

paragraphs: In stochastic shortest-path learning, an agent repeatedly tries to reach a goal at minimum expected total cost while learning unknown transition dynamics. Episode lengths are neither fixed in advance nor necessarily bounded. The agent’s actions affect how long reaching the goal takes, making this setting different from problems with predetermined episode lengths.

Earlier regret guarantees worsened as the smallest instantaneous cost decreased. This paper removes that dependence. The authors give an algorithm with regret bounded by approximately B^(3/2) S sqrt(AK), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here, B bounds the optimal policy’s expected cost, S counts states, A counts actions, and K counts episodes.

They also prove that every learning algorithm faces worst-case regret of at least order B sqrt(SAK). This lower bound provides a reference for judging how close the new algorithm comes to the best possible guarantee. Both bounds have square-root dependence on the episode count, although their dependence on B and S differs. The result strengthens the theoretical treatment of learning to reach a goal without requiring a favorable minimum step cost.
icml-2020-near-optimal-regret-bounds-for.tldr: A stochastic shortest-path algorithm removes minimum-step-cost dependence from its regret guarantee, alongside a worst-case lower bound.

paragraphs: Predicting which alternative someone will choose is important for online platforms that present users with options. The paper identifies a tension in existing choice models: some cannot represent sufficiently complex behavior, while others are difficult to apply at scale. A useful model must balance expressive power with efficient learning from data.

The authors derive a class of choice models informed by results in economics. Their framework uses set-dependent aggregation, allowing the offered set to enter the prediction process. The modeling goal is to capture complex choice patterns while preserving enough structure for statistical efficiency. They also provide a neural implementation that supports scalable, end-to-end training.

Experiments on three large choice datasets demonstrate the usefulness of the approach. The contribution combines a theoretically grounded model class with an implementation intended for substantial datasets. Its stated significance is the balance between representing richer choice behavior and retaining a structured learning problem. The experimental evidence supports that balance in the evaluated data, without establishing that the method captures every possible pattern of human choice.
icml-2020-predicting-choice-with-set-dep.tldr: A structured, set-dependent choice model combines expressive prediction with scalable neural training and demonstrates utility on three large datasets.

paragraphs: Data tracing asks whether particular samples were used to train a model. This paper proposes modifying samples imperceptibly so that training on them leaves an identifiable mark in the resulting model. The authors call these marked samples radioactive data, emphasizing that evidence of their use persists through training.

Given a trained model, the technique tests for that mark and reports a p-value expressing statistical evidence for detection. On ImageNet experiments using standard training procedures and ResNet-18, VGG-16, and DenseNet-121 architectures, the authors detect marked data with p-values below 0.0001 even when only one percent of the training data is radioactive.

The reported mark withstands strong data augmentation and changes in model architecture. The authors also report a substantially higher signal-to-noise ratio than data poisoning and backdoor methods. These findings show that small changes to a limited portion of a training set can produce a detectable training trace in the evaluated settings. The measured confidence comes from the detection test; the reported percentages and p-values describe the experiments rather than a universal detection rate.
icml-2020-radioactive-data-tracing-throu.tldr: Imperceptibly marked training samples leave detectable model traces, with high-confidence detection reported when only one percent of training data is marked.

paragraphs: A neural network’s outputs depend on its architecture and parameters in a complicated nonlinear way. That complexity can suggest that observing outputs is insufficient to reconstruct the network. This paper proves that reconstruction is frequently possible for deep ReLU networks, including their architecture, weights, and biases.

The approach exploits the piecewise linear structure of the function represented by a ReLU network. Different input regions follow different linear rules, and boundaries arise where neurons switch between inactive and active states. The authors dissect these boundaries into components associated with individual neurons. Those components provide information about both neuron weights and the neurons’ arrangement within the network.

The paper supports this reconstruction approach theoretically and empirically. Recovery is up to isomorphism, meaning that equivalent arrangements are not distinguished merely by how their components are labeled. The result does not claim that every network is always recoverable. It shows that, in the cases covered, the geometry visible through outputs contains enough information to reconstruct internal structure that might otherwise appear inaccessible.
icml-2020-reverse-engineering-deep-relu-.tldr: Deep ReLU networks can frequently be reconstructed from outputs by analyzing boundaries between their linear regions, with recovery up to isomorphism.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains representations for visual similarity, but comparing methods is difficult when training protocols, architectures, and parameter choices differ. This paper revisits widely used objective functions under a consistent comparison framework. It also studies mini-batch sampling, a training choice the authors describe as commonly overlooked.

Under those consistent comparisons, the objectives show substantially more performance saturation than the literature suggests. This finding makes the surrounding training procedure important to interpreting apparent advances. The authors also uncover a correlation between generalization performance and the density and compression of the learned embedding space, connecting performance differences with properties of the representations themselves.

Using those insights, they propose a simple training regularization that reliably improves ranking-based metric-learning models across several standard benchmark datasets. The paper therefore contributes both a reassessment of existing objectives and an empirically effective training modification. The relationship between embedding geometry and generalization is reported as a correlation; the regularization experiments provide separate evidence that acting on the identified insights can improve performance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-revisiting-training-strategies.tldr: Consistent comparisons reveal greater saturation in metric-learning objectives, while embedding-space insights motivate a regularizer that improves ranking-based models.

paragraphs: This paper provides a simpler analysis of k-means||, a distributed variant of k-means++. Its contribution concerns the number of rounds required by the algorithm. The work revisits an existing algorithm and strengthens the mathematical account of its round complexity, rather than introducing a new clustering procedure.

The authors improve the round bound from O(log n) to O(log n / log log n). The additional denominator gives a smaller asymptotic upper bound as n grows. This is a statement about how the number of rounds scales, so its significance lies in a sharper guarantee for the distributed algorithm rather than a reported measurement of execution time.

The authors also show that the new bound is tight. Thus, the analysis does more than supply a better upper bound: it establishes that the resulting order of growth captures the round requirement in the analyzed setting. Together, simplicity and tightness make the result a clearer characterization of an existing distributed method’s complexity.
icml-2020-simple-and-sharp-analysis-of-k.tldr: A simpler analysis tightens the k-means|| round bound to O(log n / log log n) and proves it tight.

paragraphs: Maximum-margin classifiers connect logistic-loss training with separating data using a particular parameter norm. This paper broadens that framework to account for structured logistic-model parameters, including sparse, block-sparse, and low-rank structures. The aim is to understand how choosing a more general objective affects classifier performance on separable data.

The proposed Generalized Margin Maximizer minimizes an arbitrary convex function of the parameters while requiring them to linearly separate the data. Classical maximum-margin classification is recovered by using the Euclidean norm. The authors provide a precise performance analysis through a system of nonlinear equations, giving a mathematical way to characterize the broader family.

They examine three cases in detail: the l2 version corresponding to the usual maximum-margin classifier, an l1 version that encourages sparsity, and an infinity-norm version often used for parameters with binary entries. Extensive simulations across parameter values, problem instances, and model structures validate the theoretical results. The contribution links the choice of convex objective to performance analysis, extending the study beyond the conventional maximum-margin formulation.
icml-2020-the-performance-analysis-of-ge.tldr: Generalized Margin Maximizers extend maximum-margin classification to arbitrary convex objectives and enable precise performance analysis for structured models.
